From an idea to a reference in a few minutes
Add your cast.
Choose the people and animals you need. Add another character whenever the scene needs one.
Start with presets.
Pick sitting, walking, a gesture or an action pose, then adjust the body if you want something more specific.
Give them a place.
Add furniture or other props. Move, rotate and resize each object until the arrangement reads clearly.
Find your view.
Orbit around the scene, use a camera shortcut, or pan with Shift + left-drag. Choose colors that make the shapes easy to distinguish.
Make the image.
Click
Pose to Image
and describe the people, setting and style. Or download the reference and use it in another image tool.
What should you put in the prompt?
Let the reference show the arrangement. Use words for the details it cannot show: who the people are, their clothes, the place, the time of day and the mood.
For a busy scene, also state how many people and animals you want. Give each one a simple description, such as “the seated person on the left” or “the cat on the stool.”
A few small choices make a big difference
Leave a gap between subjects when their arms, legs or tails overlap too much.
Check the view from the camera you will actually use. A good pose can disappear behind a table.
Use body and background colors to make your reference easy to read.
After generation, check the details that matter to you—especially hands, pet count, furniture and the crop. A reference guides the image; it does not lock every detail.

Seedance 2.0 works best when you treat video generation as a workflow, not a one-shot prompt.
A good result usually comes from four things:
clear reference assets, a structured prompt, controlled motion, and focused iteration
This tutorial walks through a practical Seedance 2.0 workflow from the first reference image to the final video.
Before writing the prompt, decide what you want Seedance to follow.
— main character, product, object, or visual style
— motion, camera movement, or action reference
— optional rhythm, dialogue, or sound reference
You do not need to use every type of reference in every generation. Start with the assets that actually affect the shot.
For example, if character appearance matters most, use a strong character image. If the camera movement is difficult to describe, add a video reference.
Sometimes you only have one image of a product, prop, or stylized object, but the video needs to show it from another angle.
Reference Image → 3D Model → Choose a New Angle → Render a Still Image → Seedance
to turn a clear object image into a 3D model, rotate the model to the angle you need, and create a new still reference. Then upload that image to Seedance as your visual anchor.
It gives you more control over the reference angle before video generation begins.
2. Write the Prompt in Three Parts
A Seedance prompt does not need to be long. It needs to be clear.
Subject and action + visual style + camera and motion
The important part is that each sentence has a job.
Describe how the scene should look:
Describe how the viewer sees it:
Combining the three gives Seedance much clearer direction than stacking unrelated adjectives.
If you upload reference files, tell Seedance what each one is for.
Do not assume the model knows why you uploaded them.
That becomes more important when several reference assets are used in the same generation.
For video generation, action logic matters more than decorative language.
These words say very little about what should actually move.
starting position → action → direction → ending position
This is especially useful when generating scenes with people, vehicles, camera movement, or several consecutive actions.
Subject movement and camera movement are different instructions.
